doc.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Race, rock and the craft of vocalese
title: How he writes lyrics and learned solos at the jukebox
summary: He writes when he hears music; as a boy he sang entire records, solos included, at Stanley Cowell Sr.'s hamburger joint for nickels.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: How do you go about your work? What is your methodology? Let’s . . .
I hear something, and I pick up the pad and pencil. It’s that simple. I hear it. I say, “Whoa.” Phew. Gone. And it’s written. I have lyrics that I haven’t even shown anybody yet.
Oh, I’m sure. Hundreds, probably.
Yeah, because I just heard the tune. I say, ooo-boy, and I write it down. I’m moved to put it down.

You must have – what is it? I want to say a photogenic [sic] memory, but it’s not that – but when you hear something, it seems to be captured. For instance, I don’t know what – how did you work in the early days? When it – since there were tapes and there were albums, but I couldn’t imagine that you always had an album to work from or a tape to work from.

Oh, no. I would work from what I heard. I would hear something. Like I used to make money to go to the movies. The movies was a dime. Popcorn was a nickel. So I would go to the local hamburger joint, Stanley’s Hamburgers, run by Stanley Cowell, the father of Stanley Cowell, the pianist.
Really?
Yeah. He ran a hamburger joint in my hometown. I knew Stanley when he was born.
I didn’t know that.

Oh yeah. I would stand if front of this jukebox. People would come up, and I’d say, “What are you going to play?” They’d say, Yard Dog Mazurka by Jimmie Lunceford. I said, “Give me the nickel. I’ll sing it for you.”
That is incredible.

They’d say, “What?” I’d say, “Give me the nickel, and I’ll sing it for you.” So just – they’d be so astounded that they would give me the nickel just to see if I could sing it, and I would sing the whole record. [Hendricks scat-sings the opening riffs of that song.] I would sing the whole record, solos and all.
That’s amazing. So you always wrote lyrics.
Yeah. I was always doing that kind of stuff.
From your earliest years.
I didn’t write lyrics to those things. I just learned them.
Okay. So you scatted them, in a sense.

Yeah, I would scat them. That’s why it was easier for me to put words to things later on, because I had been doing that. I would sing Erskine Hawkins’s Tuxedo Junction. I know that trumpet solo to this day, by Dud Bascomb. [Hendricks scat-sings the whole solo.] I love that solo. That’s one of the great solos of all time.
It stuck with you all of these years.

Oh sure. I remember that. I remember a lot of great solos that I used to sing, that people would give me the nickel here. I’d get 15 cents. I had a dime for the movie and a nickel for a big box of popcorn. You got a box of popcorn this big for a nickel. That would be my movie money.
Has your method changed over the years?
